title: Hands-On Learning: Teaching Parallel and Distributed Computing through Unplugged Activities in Undergraduate CS Courses
problem: Undergraduate CS students struggle to grasp abstract parallel computing concepts like parallelization trade-offs and performance scaling. There is a need for engaging, hands-on teaching methods to improve student understanding of parallelism principles.
motivation: Parallel computing literacy is essential for modern CS education as parallelism is increasingly critical in contemporary computing systems and applications.
method: Students in small groups used a deck of playing cards to physically simulate parallel computation, dividing the sorting task among group members and measuring how much faster they completed it together versus one person working alone. This hands-on experience showed them directly how adding more 'workers' initially speeds things up, but the speedup diminishes as the group grows—a core principle of parallelization. The activity was tested across seven courses at five institutions during 2023-2024, with surveys administered before and after to measure students' understanding.
key_novelty: Teaching how parallel computing and performance scaling work through hands-on card-sorting group activities instead of traditional lectures.
contributions: Demonstration of an effective unplugged activity for teaching parallelism and Amdahl's law concepts to undergraduates
Multi-institutional empirical evaluation showing increased student appreciation and understanding of parallelization
Practical pedagogical framework for integrating hands-on parallel computing instruction into undergraduate CS curricula
Evidence that physical simulation activities improve student grasp of parallelization trade-offs

metrics.other: Student survey responses showing increased appreciation and understanding of parallelization concepts

primary_theme: Parallel computing education through hands-on activities
